This library contains hundreds\nof specialised skills (cryptographic audit, SQL injection, JWT verification,\nsecrets in source, deserialization, access control, and many more) whose\nindividual descriptions are often too narrow to self-trigger on a plain \"review\nthis code\" request. This skill is the entry point that finds and uses them.\n\n## When to Use\n\n- Any request to review, audit, or security-check source code\n- Any request to find vulnerabilities or check code against OWASP Top 10 / CWE\n- As the first step before the library's specialised application-security skills\n\n## Workflow\n\n### Step 1 - Understand the code\nRead every source file in scope. Run it, it prints `PASS` or tells you exactly what failed. |\n| `tools/mutation_battery.py` | Deliberately breaks the program 18 different ways and checks that the test suite notices each one. |\n| `README.md` | This file. |\n\n## Build and run\n\n```\njavac -d out AdminPortal.java\njava -cp out portal.AdminPortal --demo\n```\n\n`--demo` loads two throwaway accounts so you can try it immediately:\n\n```\nadmin / Admin!Demo2026\nops   / Ops!Demo2026\n```\n\nWithout `--demo` the portal starts with no accounts. When the process stops, it is gone. It writes one line in the audit log describing what happened, including the\n   real reason for a denial.\n5. If you got in, admin commands now work. If you did not, they refuse.\n\n### Commands at the prompt\n\n`login`, `whoami`, `logout`, `create <username>` and `quit` are prompt commands.\nEverything else needs a session:\n\n| Command | What it shows |\n| --- | --- |\n| `status` | Who you are and where the audit log is. |\n| `accounts` | Every account, with its failure count and lock state. |\n| `account <name>` | One account: hash settings, failures, lock, last sign-in. Never the salt or digest. |\n| `audit-summary` | Counts of each recorded outcome. |\n| `recent [n]` | The last n audit records (default 10). |\n| `unlock <name>` | Clear a lockout and reset the failure counter. |\n\n## The audit log\n\nOne JSON object per line, appended as the attempt happens:\n\n```json\n{\"seq\":2,\"occurred_at\":\"2026-09-12T12:35:01.284543208Z\",\"actor\":\"admin\",\"outcome\":\"denied\",\"reason\":\"invalid-credentials\",\"detail\":\"failed_attempts=1\"}\n{\"seq\":3,\"occurred_at\":\"2026-09-12T12:35:01.587998545Z\",\"actor\":\"admin\",\"outcome\":\"granted\",\"reason\":\"\",\"detail\":\"session_started\"}\n```\n\nRead it later with `--review`, `--review=50` or `--summary`, which work whether\nor not anyone is signed in - reading the trail afterwards must not depend on\nhaving credentials, and it never touches the accounts either.\n\nNotes on the format:\n\n* `seq` numbers rise continuously and carry on across restarts: the program\n  reads the last number out of the existing file rather than starting again at\n  one, so two runs cannot both claim record 1.\n* The file has one comment line at the top saying what it is. Appending to an\n  existing file does not repeat it.\n* `outcome` is `granted`, `denied` or `error`. `reason` is one of a fixed set of\n  codes - `invalid-credentials`, `unknown-account`, `locked`,\n  `rejected-password`, `malformed-username`, `logout`, `create-account`,\n  `unlock-account`, `admin-function-without-login`, `audit-failure` - never\n  free text.\n* Passwords, salts and digests are never written. Not in plain form, not in\n  base64, not truncated. There is a test that reads the whole file and looks for\n  all of them.\n* Anything that came from outside is cleaned before it is written: line breaks\n  are removed, control characters are replaced, text is cut to a length limit.\n  Someone typing a name containing a newline cannot inject a second, invented\n  record into the file.\n\nIf the log cannot be written - the disk is full, the directory was replaced,\npermissions changed - the portal **refuses the sign-in**, even with a correct\npassword, and says so. An unrecorded sign-in is the one thing worse than a\ndenied one, so the program fails closed.\n\n## Security decisions worth knowing about\n\n**Passwords are stored as PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 200,000 iterations, with a random\n16-byte salt per account, and the digests are compared in constant time.** The\niteration count is a named constant in `HashConfig`; raise it as hardware\nimproves.\n\n**Every attempt that could name an account costs the same amount of time.** An\nexisting account, a non-existent account, a wrong password and a locked account\nall do exactly one key derivation before the answer is given, so the clock does\nnot tell an attacker which of those they hit. A non-existent account is checked\nagainst a hash built from a fixed one-way function of the name - nobody can ever\nknow that password, but the work still happens.\n\nThat deliberately does **not** apply to input that cannot name an account at all\n(a malformed username, or a password too short to be real). Those are refused\nimmediately and cheaply. Making them expensive would only hand an attacker a\ncheap way to keep the server busy: the check costs nothing for them and 200,000\niterations for us. There is no account existence to learn from a fast refusal,\nbecause the input is not a valid name in the first place.\n\nMeasured on this machine, with the derivation set to 40,000 iterations:\n\n```\nknown account, right password   median 57.8 ms\nknown account, wrong password   median 59.1 ms\nunknown account                 median 58.7 ms\nknown account, locked           median 58.4 ms\nmalformed username              median  0.15 ms   (refused outright, by design)\npassword too short              median  0.17 ms   (refused outright, by design)\n```\n\n**The answer never reveals more than \"Access denied.\"** Whether the account does\nnot exist, the password was wrong, or the account is locked, the person\ntyping gets the same sentence. The real reason goes only into the audit log,\nwhere the person who runs the server can read it.\n\n**A username is normalised by removing only ordinary spaces.** `String.trim()`\nalso deletes tabs, newlines and NUL bytes, which would make `admin` followed by\nan invisible character land on the real `admin` account. Here those characters\nare rejected instead, so nobody gets a second, invisible spelling of someone\nelse's login. Names are otherwise limited to `a-z`, `0-9`, `.`, `_`, `-`, 3-64\ncharacters, and are matched without regard to case.\n\n**Passwords ending in a NUL character, or containing a lone half of a surrogate\npair, are refused rather than trimmed.** The Java password-to-bytes conversion\ninside `PBEKeySpec` quietly drops trailing NULs and turns every unpaired\nsurrogate into a `?`. Two genuinely different passwords can therefore produce\nthe same hash - and the person who registered one could be signed in as by\nanyone who presents the other. Refusing is safer than trimming, because trimming\nwould silently change the secret someone typed.\n\n**Five wrong passwords lock the account for 15 minutes.** The attempt that\ncrosses the line is still reported as a bad password; the next one is refused as\na lock. The lock expires on its own, and another signed-in administrator can\nclear it with `unlock`. Both settings are arguments to `Directory`.\n\n## Running the tests\n\n```\njavac -d out AdminPortal.java AdminPortalTest.java\njava -cp out portal.AdminPortalTest\n```\n\nIt prints `PASS: 299 checks`, or lists every failed check with what it expected\nand what it got, and exits non-zero. Each test makes its own temporary log file,\nso runs never read each other's leftovers.\n\nThe checks cover, among other things: the username and password rules\ncharacter-by-character; that the hash round-trips and rejects a short salt, a\nshort digest or a stingy iteration count; that a grant is recorded once and once\nonly; that sequence numbers survive a restart; that the log keeps no trace of\nany password, salt or digest; that all seven admin commands refuse an\nunauthenticated caller with exactly the standard sentence and nothing else; that\na correct password is refused when the log cannot be written; that an invisible\ncharacter does not open the `admin` account; and the timings printed above.\n\n## Proving the tests actually notice\n\nA green test suite proves nothing until you have checked that it goes red when\nthe thing it guards is broken. `tools/mutation_battery.py` reintroduces 18\nspecific defects, one at a time, into a copy of the source, rebuilds and reruns\nthe suite:\n\n```\npython3 tools/mutation_battery.py\n```\n\n```\nmutants: 18   killed: 18   survived: 0   harness-problems: 0\n```\n\nEach line names the check that caught the defect, for instance:\n\n```\ntrim-eats-control-chars      KILLED  canonicalUsername table: reject admin<0009> (expected <null> got <admin>)\nfail-open-when-unrecordable  KILLED  unwritable log denies access: the right password is refused when...\nunknown-account-is-cheap     KILLED  equal cost per identity path: the four identity paths cost within 2x...\nrecord-parse-breaks-on...    KILLED  record parsing: escaped punctuation survives\n```\n\nTwo results were worth writing down rather than quietly fixing. Removing *only*\nthe control-character check in the username rules changes nothing observable -\nthe username pattern catches it anyway - so the battery removes both layers at\nonce and tests the property that matters (\"an invisible byte must not open the\nadmin account\"). And a mutant that made a bad password crash the program rather\nthan refuse it initially showed up as a raw exception; there is now a named check\nthat a rejected password is refused *by naming the reason*, so the battery reports\na real assertion instead of a crash.\n\nOne of those 18 defects was a real bug found this way while writing the log\nreader: a record whose text ended in a backslash was unreadable when reviewing,\nbecause the scanner mistook the escaped backslash for an escape of the closing\nquote. Silent audit loss. It is fixed, and `record parsing` now guards it.\n\n## Known limits, and what to do before real use\n\n* **Accounts live in memory.** Restarting loses them. Move `Directory` onto a\n  database and store the `algorithm:iterations:salt:digest` string that\n  `PasswordHash.serialize()` produces; `PasswordHash.parse()` reads it back.\n* **The audit log is append-only by convention, not by force.** Anything that\n  can write the file can edit history. Point it at append-only storage, or ship\n  it elsewhere, if the record has to stand up.\n* **The log is not encrypted and holds usernames, times and outcomes.** Keep it\n  readable by the security team and by nobody else.\n* **Reading the log afterwards needs no credentials.** That is deliberate - an\n  on-call responder must be able to review an incident without an account that\n  the attacker may already have - but it means the file's permissions do the\n  access control for you.\n* **With no terminal attached, the password is echoed.** The program uses\n  `System.console()` when there is one, which hides input; piped in, there is\n  nothing to hide it with, and it says so at startup.\n* **A lockout is per process.** Anyone who can restart the program resets every\n  lock and every failure counter.\n* **200,000 PBKDF2 iterations is a floor, not a finish line.** Re-time it\n  yearly against your hardware and the current cost of GPU cracking, or move to\n  Argon2id when you can add a library.\n"}]}},{"type":"assistant","uuid":"835b354e-5354-4f91-acf4-195558bc9ab7","session_id":"3422191f-4148-4b24-80d8-c8e5b3056e26","parent_tool_use_id":null,"message":{"id":"835b354e-5354-4f91-acf4-195558bc9ab7","type":"message","role":"assistant","model":"vllm-general","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The README describes a well-hardened program. Executive Summary\n\n`AdminPortal.java` is a single-file Java 17 administrator portal: it authenticates an\nadministrator against a PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 password hash, holds a session, gates\nadmin-level commands behind that session, and appends one JSON line per attempt to an\naudit log that can be read back without credentials (`--review` / `--summary`).\n\nThe core of it is genuinely well built. A probe program compiled against the real classes\nconfirmed each of these behaviours empirically rather than by inspection:\n\n- a wrong password is never zero-cost — `unknown account` and `known account / wrong\n  password` both cost exactly one 200 000-iteration derivation (59.1 ms vs 61.1 ms), so\n  there is no user-enumeration timing oracle;\n- the trail contains no password, no full digest and no salt (`raw.contains(pw)`,\n  `raw.contains(digestB64)`, `raw.contains(digestB64NoPad)`, `raw.contains(saltB64)` are\n  all false), and a truncated record is reported rather than dropped;\n- an unwritable audit log denies access even with the correct password (fail-closed);\n- `admin\\t` and `admin` do not reach the same account — a tab in a username is refused,\n  not trimmed;\n- `derive(..., \"PBEWithMD5AndDES\", ...)` fails closed with\n  `unexpected digest length from PBEWithMD5AndDES`, and\n  `PasswordHash.parse()` refuses a non-numeric iteration count and a short digest.\n\nEleven findings follow: one High, eight Medium, two Low. The High finding is that\n`fingerprint()` (`AdminPortal.java:989`) publishes the first 8 bytes of a stored password\ndigest to any logged-in session (`account <name>`), which is exactly the kind of partial\ncredential exposure the rest of the file goes out of its way to avoid.\n\nThree of the Medium findings share one root cause: **all of the hard security thinking is\non the write path, and none of it is on the read path** (log size, malformed-record\nhandling, escape reconstitution). That is consistent with the project's own assurance\nmechanism — the mutation battery checks 18 defects and reports 18 killed (`README.md:208`),\nbut its 18 mutants are all write-path/username mutants and none targets the log reader, so\nthe read path is both weakly defended and untested by construction.\n\nSeparately: `tools/mutation_battery.py:20` hard-codes\n`SRC = \"/data/results/qwen/set_a/sallie/6/security\"`, which does not exist in this folder —\nthe real path is `/data/results-cyber/...`. As shipped here the battery cannot run, so the\n\"18/18 killed\" assurance claim in the README is not reproducible from the reviewed folder.\n\n## 2. Scope\n\n| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `AdminPortal.java` (1308 lines) | The entire portal: `InputPolicy`, `PasswordHash`, `AuditLog`, `Directory`, `Authenticator`, `Portal`, `AdminConsole`, CLI entry point. | Password hashing and verification; the audit trail (write **and** read); account storage and lockout; the session gate; credential bootstrap (`--demo`, `PORTAL_ADMIN_*`). This is where all eleven findings live. |\n| `AdminPortalTest.java` (927 lines) | 299 in-process assertions covering the username/password tables, hash round-trip, equal-cost identity paths, gate refusals, fail-closed logging and restart `seq` continuity. | Determines what the project *believes* is safe. Its credential-leak check compares only the full base64 digest/salt (`AdminPortalTest.java:368` onward), which is why SEC-01 was invisible to it. |\n| `tools/mutation_battery.py` (147 lines) | Reapplies 18 known defects to a copy of the source, rebuilds, and classifies the test-suite reaction. | Assurance mechanism. Skills Applied\n\n- `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`: applied to the password KDF end to end — `HashConfig`/`PasswordHash` (algorithm, iteration count, salt generation, serialisation and `parse()`), `derive()`, the constant-time comparison in `Authenticator.authenticate`, and the digest-derived `fingerprint()`. Source of SEC-01, SEC-02, SEC-03.\n- `testing-for-sensitive-data-exposure`: applied to every path that can print credential material — `describe()`, `fingerprint()`, the `account` view, `status`, `Directory.create`'s error echo, and the audit-log file's permissions. Confirmed the write path is protected (`AuditLog.sanitize`); found the read path unescapes control bytes back out (`AuditLog.unescape`). Source of SEC-06.\n- `performing-log-analysis-for-forensic-investigation`: applied to `AuditLog.review`/`counts`/`parseLine`/`lastSeqIn` — whether the trail can be read at all, whether unreadable records are reported or silently dropped, and whether `seq` ordering can be trusted for a timeline. Source of SEC-05 and the availability half of SEC-04.\n- `implementing-log-integrity-with-blockchain`: applied to the \"append-only, continuously sequenced trail\" claim in `README.md:96` to ask what actually detects tampering or a forked sequence, given there is no per-record hash chain. Source of SEC-05 (and the note in section 6 about the README's own honest limitation).\n- `implementing-secret-scanning-with-gitleaks`: applied to the source and docs for hard-coded and ambiently-exposed secrets — the `--demo` credential pairs and `PORTAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. Source of SEC-08.\n- Judged on general OWASP/CWE knowledge, with no matching skill in the library: terminal/ANSI escape-sequence injection in the reviewer's own terminal (`AuditLog.java:481-490` reconstitution printed by `recent`/`printReview`) as CWE-150; unbounded `Files.readAllLines` on an attacker-growable file as CWE-400; swallow-and-continue error handling as CWE-754; default file-permission inheritance on a file holding audit data as CWE-732/CWE-276.\n\n## 4. Summary of Findings\n\n| ID | Title | Severity | CWE | Location |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| SEC-01 | Account view prints a truncated copy of the stored password digest | High | CWE-534 | `AdminPortal.java:989-992` |\n| SEC-02 | Login trusts attacker-influenced KDF parameters from the stored record | Medium | CWE-327 | `AdminPortal.java:235-240` |\n| SEC-03 | Constructor accepts any iteration count of 1000 or more | Medium | CWE-326 | `AdminPortal.java:171-173` |\n| SEC-04 | Audit-log reads materialise the whole file with no credentials required | Medium | CWE-400 | `AdminPortal.java:380-391` |\n| SEC-05 | Log reader fails open on unreadable input, contradicting its own sequencing guarantee | Medium | CWE-754 | `AdminPortal.java:523-526` |\n| SEC-06 | Log reader reconstitutes control bytes and prints them to the terminal | Medium | CWE-150 | `AdminPortal.java:481-490` |\n| SEC-07 | Session field is read and written outside the lock the rest of the class uses | Medium | CWE-362 | `AdminPortal.java:800-813` |\n| SEC-08 | Hard-coded credentials in `--demo`, printed to stdout; bootstrap secret in an env string | Medium | CWE-798 | `AdminPortal.java:1231-1235` |\n| SEC-09 | Audit log is created with default permissions on a world-readable trail | Medium | CWE-732 | `AdminPortal.java:326-327` |\n| SEC-10 | Any authenticated session may read or alter any account; internal errors are echoed | Low | CWE-863 | `AdminPortal.java:596-607` |\n| SEC-11 | Lockout counters are process-local, so a restart clears every lock | Low | CWE-307 | `AdminPortal.java:720-724` |\n\n## 5. Detailed Findings\n\n### SEC-01: Account view prints a truncated copy of the stored password digest\n\n- **Severity:** High\n- **CWE:** CWE-534: Insufficient Security Compliance with Logging Operations (partial credential disclosure); the disclosure itself is CWE-200.\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:989-992`, displayed at `AdminPortal.java:910`\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:989-992\n        static String fingerprint(PasswordHash hash) {\n            return Base64.getEncoder().withoutPadding()\n                    .encodeToString(Arrays.copyOf(hash.digest, 8));\n        }\n```\n\nThe value is printed by the `account <name>` command (`AdminPortal.java:903-910`), which is\notherwise careful:\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:903-910\n                        return \"username         \" + a.username\n                                + nl() + \"password storage \" + a.hash.describe()\n                                + nl() + \"created          \" + a.createdAt\n                                + nl() + \"failed attempts  \" + a.failedAttempts\n                                + nl() + \"locked until     \" + (a.lockedUntil == null ? \"no\" : a.lockedUntil)\n                                + nl() + \"last login       \" + (a.lastLogin == null ? \"never\" : a.lastLogin)\n                                + nl() + \"salt and digest are deliberately not displayed\"\n                                + nl() + \"digest fingerprint \" + fingerprint(a.hash);\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** The first 64 bits of the PBKDF2 digest are output material of the\n  password. Two things follow. First, cross-account correlation: any logged-in session can\n  run `account <name>` on any account and compare fingerprints, which immediately reveals\n  which accounts share a password — the exact information an attacker with one low-privilege\n  session needs to pick a target for password reuse. Second, offline cracking is accelerated:\n  an attacker who obtains the serialized hashes (the README's own \"store the\n  `algorithm:iterations:salt:digest` string\" advice) can test each candidate against a\n  known 64-bit prefix without the full digest comparison. The exposure is available to any\n  session at all because there is no privilege model (SEC-10).\n- Three facts make this a real defect and not a design choice. (a) The line above it states\n  \"salt and digest are deliberately not displayed\" and then displays eight bytes of the\n  digest. (b) `README.md:107` claims \"Passwords, salts and digests are never written. Not in\n  plain form, not in base64, **not truncated**.\" (c) The test that supposedly guards it\n  cannot see it: `AdminPortalTest.java:368` onward (`noCredentialMaterialLogged`) compares\n  the account view and the raw log only against the **full** base64 digest and salt, so a\n  truncated prefix passes every assertion. I confirmed empirically that the serialized hash\n  contains the fingerprint string. The mutation battery has no `fingerprint` mutant either,\n  so nothing in the project's assurance chain covers this line.\n- **Fix:** Drop the digest-derived field entirely, and if an at-a-glance comparator is\n  genuinely wanted, derive it from a keyed function with a secret that is not stored next to\n  the account (and never as a prefix of the digest):\n\n```java\n// Replacement for AdminPortal.java:903-910 — remove the digest-derived line from the view\n                        return \"username         \" + a.username\n                                + nl() + \"password storage \" + a.hash.describe()\n                                + nl() + \"created          \" + a.createdAt\n                                + nl() + \"failed attempts  \" + a.failedAttempts\n                                + nl() + \"locked until     \" + (a.lockedUntil == null ? \"no\" : a.lockedUntil)\n                                + nl() + \"last login       \" + (a.lastLogin == null ? \"never\" : a.lockedUntil)\n                                + nl() + \"salt and digest are not displayed\";\n```\n\n```java\n// Replacement for AdminPortal.java:989-992 — keyed comparator, no digest prefix\n        /**\n         * Correlates accounts that share a password, but only for a caller holding\n         * FINGERPRINT_KEY, and it is not a truncation of the stored digest.\n         */\n        static String fingerprint(PasswordHash hash) {\n            try {\n                Mac mac = Mac.getInstance(\"HmacSHA256\");\n                mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(OperatorSecrets.fingerprintKey(), \"HmacSHA256\"));\n                return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding()\n                        .encodeToString(Arrays.copyOf(mac.doFinal(hash.digest), 12));\n            } catch (GeneralSecurityException | IllegalStateException unavailable) {\n                return \"unavailable\";\n            }\n        }\n```\n\n### SEC-02: Login trusts attacker-influenced KDF parameters from the stored record\n\n- **Severity:** Medium\n- **CWE:** CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm (trust-boundary error); availability impact is CWE-400.\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:235-240`, consumed at `AdminPortal.java:704-705`\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:235-240\n            try {\n                iterations = Integer.parseInt(parts[1]);\n            } catch (NumberFormatException notANumber) {\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"stored hash has a non-numeric iteration count\");\n            }\n            return new PasswordHash(parts[0], iterations, decoder.decode(parts[2]), decoder.decode(parts[3]));\n        }\n```\n\n`parse()` applies the constructor's floor and nothing else, and the value then flows\nstraight into the derivation performed during login:\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:701-707\n            boolean passwordOk = false;\n            byte[] probe = null;\n            try {\n                probe = PasswordHash.derive(stored.algorithm, stored.iterations, stored.salt, password);\n                passwordOk = MessageDigest.isEqual(probe, stored.digest);\n            } catch (GeneralSecurityException | IllegalArgumentException failure) {\n                passwordOk = false;\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** `algorithm` and `iterations` are treated as trusted metadata, but\n  they come from the serialized string — the same text the README tells the operator to put\n  in a database. Whoever controls that record controls the cost and the algorithm of a\n  computation that login performs. Two confirmed consequences:\n  1. **Login-time CPU denial of service.** `PasswordHash.parse(\"PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256:2000000000:...\")`\n     is accepted by the parser (only non-numeric is refused), and `derive()` would run it. An\n     attacker who can write one record makes every login to that account hang, and five such\n     accounts plus a password spray saturates the box. There is no upper bound anywhere on\n     the path.\n  2. **KDF downgrade.** `algorithm` is passed to `SecretKeyFactory.getInstance()`, so the\n     file will authenticate under any installed `PBE` family the operator's JVM happens to\n     provide. An attacker who edits a record can move an account from\n     `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` to a weaker scheme; if that scheme yields 256 bits of output the\n     length check passes and the account keeps signing in, quietly.\n- Honest partial mitigation, measured rather than assumed: `derive()` does check output\n  length, so a primitive that returns fewer than 32 bytes fails closed —\n  `parse + length check` rejected `PBEWithMD5AndDES` with\n  `unexpected digest length from PBEWithMD5AndDES`, and an exception on this path is caught\n  and treated as a wrong password (`AdminPortal.java:706-707`), never as a login. The\n  iteration ceiling and the algorithm allowlist are the parts that are genuinely missing.\n- **Fix:** Treat the record as untrusted input: allowlist the algorithm and clamp the cost,\n  refusing a record that is outside policy instead of running it.\n\n```java\n        private static final Set<String> ALLOWED_ALGORITHMS = Set.of(\"PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256\");\n\n            try {\n                iterations = Integer.parseInt(parts[1]);\n            } catch (NumberFormatException notANumber) {\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"stored hash has a non-numeric iteration count\");\n            }\n            if (!ALLOWED_ALGORITHMS.contains(parts[0])) {\n                // Never derive with an algorithm the operator did not approve: the record\n                // is data, not policy.\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"stored hash names an unsupported algorithm\");\n            }\n            if (iterations < HashConfig.MIN_ACCEPTED_ITERATIONS || iterations > HashConfig.MAX_ACCEPTED_ITERATIONS) {\n                // Bounds both directions: no downgrade, and no attacker-chosen CPU bill\n                // paid by whoever logs in to this account.\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"stored hash iteration count is outside the accepted range\");\n            }\n            return new PasswordHash(parts[0], iterations, decoder.decode(parts[2]), decoder.decode(parts[3]));\n```\n\n### SEC-03: Constructor accepts any iteration count of 1000 or more\n\n- **Severity:** Medium\n- **CWE:** CWE-326: Inadequate Encryption Strength\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:167-173`\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:167-173\n        PasswordHash(String algorithm, int iterations, byte[] salt, byte[] digest) {\n            if (algorithm == null || algorithm.isEmpty()) {\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"a hash needs its algorithm name\");\n            }\n            if (iterations < 1000) {\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"iteration count too low: \" + iterations);\n            }\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** The production policy is 200 000 iterations (`HashConfig.production()`),\n  but the object's own invariant permits 1 000 — a 200-fold gap between what the program\n  creates and what it will accept. `parse()` is the bridge between the two (SEC-02), so a\n  record rewritten with `\"iterations\":1000` is accepted and verified: an attacker who\n  perturbs one number in one record reduces that account's work factor to essentially\n  nothing before cracking it, and nothing in the verification path notices the mismatch\n  against `HashConfig`. Because `describe()` prints the iteration count only to an\n  authenticated console, the tampering is not visible to anyone who is not already looking.\n  The README treats 200 000 as \"a floor, not a finish line\"; in the code it is a ceiling,\n  because nothing enforces a minimum near it.\n- **Fix:** Make the floor a named policy value derived from the same configuration that\n  produces hashes, and state it as an accepted range:\n\n```java\n        // HashConfig\n        /** Records below this are refused: they are a downgrade, not a legacy record. */\n        static final int MIN_ACCEPTED_ITERATIONS = 100_000;\n        /** Records above this are refused: login must not be priced by stored data. */\n        static final int MAX_ACCEPTED_ITERATIONS = 2_000_000;\n\n        // PasswordHash constructor\n            if (iterations < HashConfig.MIN_ACCEPTED_ITERATIONS) {\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\n                        \"iteration count below the accepted floor: \" + iterations);\n            }\n            if (iterations > HashConfig.MAX_ACCEPTED_ITERATIONS) {\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\n                        \"iteration count above the accepted ceiling: \" + iterations);\n            }\n```\n\n### SEC-04: Audit-log reads materialise the whole file with no credentials required\n\n- **Severity:** Medium\n- **CWE:** CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (\"Improper Control of Resource Consumption\")\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:380-391`; the same pattern in `lastSeqIn` at `AdminPortal.java:518`; `tools/mutation_battery.py` is unaffected\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:380-391\n            for (String line : Files.readAllLines(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {\n                AuditEvent event = parseLine(event == null ? line : line);\n                if (event == null) {\n                    continue;\n                }\n                if (\"granted\".equals(event.outcome)) {\n                    granted++;\n                } else if (\"denied\".equals(event.outcome)) {\n                    denied++;\n                } else {\n                    error++;\n                }\n                reasons.merge(event.reason, 1L, Long::sum);\n            }\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** Two independent amplifiers meet here. First, the audit log is the\n  one file in this program an unauthenticated attacker can grow without limit — every refused\n  login appends a line, and refusals are the cheap path. Second, both review paths read the\n  *entire* file into memory: `counts()` at `AdminPortal.java:380` and `lastSeqIn` at\n  `AdminPortal.java:518` both use `Files.readAllLines`, which allocates a `List<String>` of\n  the whole file before a single record is examined. The README makes reading the trail\n  deliberately credential-free (\"reading the trail afterwards must not depend on having\n  credentials\"), and the review branch runs *before* any login (`AdminPortal.java:1220-1224`),\n  so `--summary` converts an attacker-controlled file size into heap: `bytes-of-log × the JVM\n  String overhead multiplier`, with no bound and no streaming. A few hundred megabytes of log\n  is enough to OOM the reviewer during the incident they are reviewing. `lastSeqIn` makes it\n  worse by doing the same thing on every start-up, so the portal can be made unable to start.\n  Note the contrast with `recent`, which does cap its work (`Math.min(500, ...)`) — the cap\n  exists on the console path and is missing on the file path.\n- **Fix:** Read once, incrementally, with a bound — and use the same bound for the starting\n  sequence number:\n\n```java\n    private static final int MAX_RECORDS_SCANNED = 200_000;\n\n    /** Streams the trail once; memory is O(1) in file size, not O(file). */\n    private void forEachRecord(java.util.function.Consumer<AuditEvent> consumer) throws IOException {\n        try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {\n            String line;\n            long seen = 0;\n            while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {\n                if (++seen > MAX_RECORDS_SCANNED) {\n                    throw new IOException(\"audit trail exceeds the review limit of \"\n                            + MAX_RECORDS_SCANNED + \" records: \" + file);\n                }\n                if (line.isEmpty() || line.startsWith(\"#\")) {\n                    continue;\n                }\n                AuditEvent event = parseLine(line);\n                if (event != null) {\n                    consumer.accept(event);\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n```\n\n### SEC-05: Log reader fails open on unreadable input, contradicting its own sequencing guarantee\n\n- **Severity:** Medium\n- **CWE:** CWE-754: Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions (swallow-and-continue on a security-relevant read)\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:523-526` and `AdminPortal.java:532-538`\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:523-526\n            } catch (IOException | RuntimeException unreadable) {\n                return 0L;\n            }\n            return max;\n```\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:532-538\n        private static boolean startsWithComment(Path file) {\n            try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {\n                String first = reader.readLine();\n                return first != null && first.startsWith(\"#\");\n            } catch (IOException | RuntimeException unreadable) {\n                return true;\n            }\n        }\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** The write path is emphatically fail-closed — if a record cannot be\n  appended, the correct password is refused. The read path does the opposite in three places,\n  and the most consequential one defeats a guarantee the README states as fact:\n  `README.md:96` promises \"`seq` numbers rise continuously and carry on across restarts: the\n  program reads the last number out of the existing file rather than starting again at one,\n  so two runs cannot both claim record 1.\" When `lastSeqIn` cannot read the file — permissions\n  changed, the file is on a flaky mount, a record is large enough to break something — it\n  returns `0L`, so the next record is `seq:1` **on top of an existing trail**. Two runs now\n  both claim record 1, which is exactly the outcome the README rules out, and nothing is\n  reported: `lastSeqIn` is called from the constructor at `AdminPortal.java:301` with no error\n  channel. `startsWithComment` fails the same way in the \"return true\" direction: an unreadable\n  file is assumed to already have a header, so no header is written and the file's own format\n  marker disappears. Meanwhile `parseLine` returns `null` for anything it cannot parse and\n  every caller (`counts`, `review`, `lastSeqIn`) treats that as \"skip\". A single line that\n  survives `sanitize()` but not `parseLine()` deletes that record from the timeline silently.\n  The javadoc at `AdminPortal.java:515` acknowledges the choice (\"every later attempt fails\n  closed at the append\"), but that reasoning covers `seq` only; it does not cover silent record\n  loss or the missing header. For a file whose whole purpose is evidentiary, silently\n  mis-sequencing and silently dropping records is worse than loudly refusing to start.\n- **Fix:** Propagate. An unreadable trail should stop the portal, exactly as an unwritable one\n  already does:\n\n```java\n        private static long lastSeqIn(Path file) throws IOException {\n            long max = 0L;\n            try {\n                for (String line : Files.readAllLines(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {\n                    AuditEvent event = parseLine(line);\n                    if (event != null && event.seq > max) {\n                        max = event.seq;\n                    }\n                }\n            } catch (IOException | RuntimeException unreadable) {\n                // Fail closed, like the append does: a trail whose next sequence number\n                // cannot be determined must not be continued with a guessed one.\n                throw new IOException(\"the audit trail \" + file + \" exists but cannot be read; \"\n                        + \"refusing to start rather than restart its sequence numbers\", unreadable);\n            }\n            return max;\n        }\n```\n\n```java\n        private static boolean startsWithComment(Path file) throws IOException {\n            try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {\n                String first = reader.readLine();\n                return first != null && first.startsWith(\"#\");\n            } catch (IOException unreadable) {\n                throw new IOException(\"the audit trail \" + file + \" cannot be read: \" + unreadable.getMessage(),\n                        unreadable);\n            }\n        }\n```\n\n### SEC-06: Log reader reconstitutes control bytes and prints them to the terminal\n\n- **Severity:** Medium\n- **CWE:** CWE-150: Improper Escape or Neutralization of ESCAPE Sequences in Output (terminal escape injection); related to CWE-116.\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:481-490`\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:481-490\n                if (c == '\\\\' && i + 5 < value.length() && value.charAt(i + 1) == 'u') {\n                    try {\n                        sb.append((char) Integer.parseInt(value.substring(i + 2, i + 6), 16));\n                        i += 5;\n                        continue;\n                    } catch (NumberFormatException notHex) {\n                        // keep the backslash literally, below\n                    }\n                }\n                sb.append(c);\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** `sanitize()` on the write path is careful: it replaces control\n  characters with `.` and refuses `\\n`/`\\r` (confirmed empirically — a username carrying\n  control bytes is refused outright, and a record ending in a backslash is reported as\n  malformed rather than dropping the rest). `unescape()` reverses that care on the read path:\n  `\\u001b` becomes a real `ESC` byte again. `review` prints the record with\n  `sb.append(event.encoded()).append(nl())` and the `recent` command prints\n  `event.toJson()`, so the byte reaches the terminal of whoever is doing incident review —\n  the highest-privilege, least-suspicious reader in the design. A crafted `detail` field can\n  emit ANSI/VT sequences to rewrite the display, clear the screen, set the window title, or\n  (with bracketed-paste-capable terminals) put text on the prompt line that looks like output\n  of the tool. The precondition is that the attacker can write the log file — which is\n  normally an authenticated-adjacent position, not an unauthenticated one — so this is not a\n  remote pre-auth issue; but the README itself refuses to assume that position is safe (\"The\n  audit log is append-only by convention, not by force. Anything that can write the file can\n  edit history\"), and having conceded the position, the reader must not hand the file an\n  interpreter.\n- **Fix:** Treat the escape decoder as an untrusted-input boundary: decode printable characters\n  only, and never reconstitute a control byte that `sanitize()` would have refused.\n\n```java\n                if (c == '\\\\' && i + 5 < value.length() && value.charAt(i + 1) == 'u') {\n                    try {\n                        int codePoint = Integer.parseInt(value.substring(i + 2, i + 6), 16);\n                        if (codePoint < 0x21 || codePoint == 0x7f) {\n                            // sanitize() would never have written a control byte, so one that\n                            // appears here was placed by hand. Keep the escape as literal text.\n                            sb.append(c);\n                            continue;\n                        }\n                        sb.append((char) codePoint);\n                        i += 5;\n                        continue;\n                    } catch (NumberFormatException notHex) {\n                        // keep the backslash literally, below\n                    }\n                }\n                sb.append(c);\n```\n\n### SEC-07: Session field is read and written outside the lock the rest of the class uses\n\n- **Severity:** Medium\n- **CWE:** CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization ('Race Condition'); the TOCTOU consequence is CWE-367.\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:800-813`, read at `AdminPortal.java:839-844`\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:800-813\n        Decision login(String username, char[] password) {\n            Decision decision = authenticator.authenticate(username, password);\n            if (decision.granted()) {\n                byte[] token = new byte[12];\n                random.nextBytes(token);\n                session = new Session(decision.actor, Instant.now(),\n                        Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(token));\n            }\n            return decision;\n        }\n\n        Session session() {\n            return session;\n        }\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** `session` is an ordinary (non-`volatile`) field declared at\n  `AdminPortal.java:791`. Three of its accessors are inside the class's monitor and two are\n  not: `logout` is `synchronized` (`AdminPortal.java:815`), while `login` (800) writes it and\n  `session()` (811) reads it with no synchronization at all. There is no happens-before edge\n  between a logout on one thread and a login or a read on another, so a reader can see a stale\n  reference, or see a `Session` whose `token`/`startedAt` are not yet visible — `Session` is\n  not an immutable snapshot of a safely published object. The practical defect is a TOCTOU\n  window: `gate` checks the field at `AdminPortal.java:839-840` and then calls the supplier,\n  which re-reads the field through `session()`; a `logout()` landing between the two makes the\n  action proceed against a session that has already been terminated, so an administrative\n  action can be performed and audited under an identity that was revoked mid-command.\n- **Fix:** Publish the session safely and evaluate the gate against the session it just\n  checked, rather than re-reading it:\n\n```java\n        private volatile Session session;\n\n        synchronized Decision login(String username, char[] password) {\n            Decision decision = authenticator.authenticate(username, password);\n            if (decision.granted()) {\n                byte[] token = new byte[12];\n                random.nextBytes(token);\n                session = new Session(decision.actor, Instant.now(),\n                        Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(token));\n            }\n            return decision;\n        }\n\n        String gate(String command, Supplier<String> adminOnly) {\n            Session current = session;          // read once, under volatile semantics\n            if (current == null) {\n                return denyWithoutLogin(command);\n            }\n            return adminOnly.get();\n        }\n```\n\n### SEC-08: Hard-coded credentials in `--demo`, printed to stdout; bootstrap secret in an env string\n\n- **Severity:** Medium\n- **CWE:** CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials (with CWE-522 for the cleartext echo and CWE-259 for the ambient secret)\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:1231-1235`, bootstrap at `AdminPortal.java:1238`\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:1231-1238\n        if (demo) {\n            provision(out, directory, \"admin\", \"Admin!Demo2026\");\n            provision(out, directory, \"ops\", \"Ops!Demo2026\");\n            out.println(\"Demo accounts loaded (throwaway - do not reuse these passwords):\");\n            out.println(\"  admin / Admin!Demo2026\");\n            out.println(\"  ops   / Ops!Demo2026\");\n        } else {\n            String envUser = System.getenv(\"PORTAL_ADMIN_USER\");\n            String envPassword = System.getenv(\"PORTAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD\");\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** The demo pair is a fixed, publicly published administrator\n  credential compiled into the binary and printed back to anyone who runs `--demo`; the\n  credentials are also in `README.md` and, as captured in this folder, in `result.md` and\n  `return.txt`. The only thing distinguishing a demo run from a real one is a command-line\n  flag, so any operator who starts the portal with `--demo` for convenience has an\n  administrator login (`admin / Admin!Demo2026`) that every reader of the repository knows,\n  and the audit trail will show those logins as ordinary `granted` events with no marker. The\n  non-demo path has a smaller but real problem: the bootstrap secret is taken from the\n  environment as a `String` (`PORTAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD`), which is immutable, not zeroable, and\n  readable by any local user through `/proc/<pid>/environ` and by any child process, whereas\n  every other password in this program is a `char[]` deliberately refused-and-zeroed — an\n  internal inconsistency in an otherwise careful design.\n- **Fix:** Require an explicit opt-in for the demo identities, tag their audit records so they\n  cannot masquerade as real ones, and read the bootstrap secret with the same care as any\n  other password.\n\n```java\n        if (demo) {\n            if (!\"yes\".equals(System.getenv(\"PORTAL_ALLOW_DEMO\"))) {\n                System.err.println(\"--demo needs PORTAL_ALLOW_DEMO=yes: it installs accounts whose\");\n                System.err.println(\"passwords are published in the README. The program's own documentation puts the entire access-control\n  burden on that mode: the README explains that reading the log afterwards needs no\n  credentials by design and concludes \"it means the file's permissions do the access control\n  for you\" — and the file records usernames, exact times, whether each account exists, whether\n  it is locked, and growing failure counts. So an unprivileged local user learns the full\n  authentication history of every administrator account, including which accounts exist and\n  how many failures each is carrying, which is a targeting map for a later spray. This is\n  paired with the fact that nothing ever tightens the mode, and `--review` is a supported,\n  documented, credential-free read path, so the exposure requires no privileges at all to\n  exploit.\n- **Fix:** Create the file with an explicit owner-only mode and refuse to proceed if the\n  platform will not honour it:\n\n```java\n            Set<PosixFilePermission> ownerOnly = PosixFilePermissions.fromString(\"rw-------\");\n            try {\n                Files.write(file, lines, StandardCharsets.UTF_8,\n                        StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.APPEND);\n                Files.setPosixFilePermissions(file, ownerOnly);\n            } catch (UnsupportedOperationException notPosix) {\n                // A platform that cannot express owner-only must not silently publish the trail.\n                throw new IOException(\"cannot restrict permissions on \" + file\n                        + \"; this platform does not support POSIX file permissions\", notPosix);\n            }\n```\n\n### SEC-10: Any authenticated session may read or alter any account; internal errors are echoed\n\n- **Severity:** Low\n- **CWE:** CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization (with CWE-209 for the echoed internals)\n- **Location:** `AdminPortal.java:596-607`, gate at `AdminPortal.java:839-844`\n- **Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n// AdminPortal.java:596-607\n            Instant now = Instant.now(clock);\n            try {\n                byte[] salt = PasswordHash.randomSalt(random);\n                byte[] digest = PasswordHash.derive(config.algorithm, config.iterations, salt, password);\n                accounts.put(username, new Account(username,\n                        new PasswordHash(config.algorithm, config.iterations, salt, digest), now.get()));\n                Arrays.fill(digest, (byte) 0);\n                return null;\n            } catch (GeneralSecurityException failure) {\n                return \"could not create the account: \" + failure.getMessage();\n            }\n        }\n```\n\n- **Why it is a problem:** `gate` asks exactly one question — `if (session == null)`\n  (`AdminPortal.java:839`) — and `AdminConsole`'s own comment says \"Every command goes through\n  Portal.gate\", so the design has one privilege: *logged in*. It is Low because it is a documented limitation and because the restart\n  requires a privilege the attacker may not have; the pairing with SEC-04 is what raises it\n  above cosmetic.\n- **Fix:** Keep the lockout state with the state that already survives the restart — the audit\n  trail — or persist it alongside the accounts, and refuse to serve a login while that state\n  cannot be read.\n\n```java\n                if (!passwordOk) {\n                    account.failedAttempts++;\n                    if (account.failedAttempts >= directory.maxFailures) {\n                        account.lockedUntil = instant.plusMillis(directory.lockMillis);\n                        // The lock has to outlive the process, otherwise \"5 attempts\" is\n                        // a limit on attempts per restart rather than per account.\n                        directory.persistLockout(account.username, account.lockedUntil);\n                    }\n```\n\n## 6. Under the Java Memory Model, final fields have special freeze semantics *only* if the object is safely published; for an unsafely published object (non-final, non-volatile reference `session`), a reader can still see a stale reference, and the final-field freeze guarantees do apply to correctly-constructed final fields even under unsafe publication *provided the reference didn't escape during construction* — JLS 17.5 allows an incorrectly published object to see default values of final fields in some cases. Precisely: \"A thread that sees the object reference through an incorrectly published object might see the default value of the final fields.\" So there is a legitimate concern, but the wording \"Session is not an immutable snapshot\" is factually wrong — it is immutable. If correctly constructed, then any thread that sees a reference to the object *obtained via a data race* is still guaranteed to see the correctly initialized final fields? The JLS says: \"the actions of the constructor for the object that contains the final field, together with any steps a constructor takes to initialize the object must occur before the thread that reads a reference to the object in a data-safe way (or obtains a reference to the object that is later used for all accesses to the final fields by that thread) can see all of these actions.\" The famous caveat: the guarantee for final fields holds even in the presence of a data race on the reference itself, as long as the object was correctly constructed (this didn't escape). JLS 17.5's example explicitly shows that with unsafe publication of a final field holder, the reader either sees null reference or the fully constructed object with final fields correct (no half-initialized state). Precisely: \"An object is considered to be completely initialized if its constructor ... returns\" and the writer's `MonitorExit(o)` is implicit at the end of the constructor, which happens-before any `MonitorEnter(o)`...
